narrative: The model estimates a 92% probability that you will leave your job, so the promotion decision is currently denied because the organization expects you may not be there to take on the role. This is a probability, not a certainty, and it is not a judgment of your ability; it is a retention-risk prediction. The strongest signal was your total years of experience: at 6–10 years, you differ from the many employees predicted to stay who have only 1–5 years, and this pushed the forecast toward leaving. The second signal was that you have other job opportunities; most employees predicted to stay reported none, so this materially raised the leave risk. The third was your 1–5 years in the current organization; although that tenure is common among stayers, in your overall profile it still added to the leaving signal. Together, these signals made departure look much more likely than staying. Before treating the denial as final, you and the organization should discuss concrete retention steps: clarify promotion criteria and timing, review career progression and recognition, address job stability and workload, and explore whether external opportunities reflect unmet needs. The organization should also check support, engagement, work–life balance, and satisfaction, because improving these may lower leave risk and make promotion viable.
